tldr: By using the 3D geometric motion of the wrist and grasp center in camera coordinates as a common language, this study enables a single base policy to learn across completely different embodiments—single-arm, dual-arm, humanoid, and human hands—and control diverse robots without additional fine-tuning.
hero_caption: Overall framework of UCAG-P. It aligns actions across different embodiments—such as single-arm, dual-arm, humanoid, and human hands—into a shared geometric space defined by the 3D trajectories of the wrist and grasp center in camera coordinates, and then converts them into executable joint commands via a target-embodiment translator.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly generate robot actions from vision and language have garnered significant attention, but scaling them with massive data faces a major bottleneck: embodiment heterogeneity. Real-world and simulated datasets encompass single-arm robots, dual-arm robots, humanoids, and human task videos. Each features different camera configurations, degrees of freedom, and low-level control commands such as joint angles or end-effector velocities. Conventionally, policies required embodiment-specific output heads, video-to-video synthesis, or retargeting to force motions into a specific robot form, hindering the training of a truly unified model.

The authors focused on the insight that the most universal shared structure lies not in low-level control commands, but in the camera-observable geometric action of manipulation itself. Whether human or robot, task progress can be described by how the wrist (end-effector) and the grasp center move from the camera's perspective. Based on this idea, they propose UCAG-P. UCAG-P represents diverse robot and human hand motions within a shared space of two-point anchor motion in camera-frame coordinates, allowing the base policy to learn geometric task progress. For actual robot control, a geometry-conditioned action translator combines the camera-frame motion with the target embodiment's kinematics and Jacobian matrices to generate executable joint commands.

Trained on a massive dataset of over 6,300 hours spanning simulation and real robots, a single unified checkpoint achieved a 98.3% success rate on LIBERO, around 89% on RoboTwin, and 62.0% on the humanoid benchmark RoboCasa GR-1. It achieved these results without any benchmark-specific fine-tuning while also demonstrating strong adaptation capabilities on real robots.
contributions: Proposed UCAG-P, which unifies incompatible action spaces across single-arm, dual-arm, humanoid, and human hands into a shared camera-centric geometric space of two-point anchor motion.
Enabled human manipulation videos to be directly incorporated as an independent embodiment into the shared geometric space without synthesizing robot videos.
Developed a decoupled geometry-conditioned action translator that produces executable control commands from shared geometric predictions using target kinematics and Jacobians.
Achieved state-of-the-art success rates on diverse benchmarks such as LIBERO, RoboTwin, and RoboCasa using a single model checkpoint without individual fine-tuning.

sections.heading: How Can We Bridge Heterogeneous Embodiments?: A Shared Language of Camera-Centric Geometry
sections.summary: Scaling robot manipulation across large datasets has been hindered by disparate morphologies and action spaces. This paper solves the issue by introducing wrist and grasp-center camera-frame motions as a unified representation, decoupling task geometry from embodiment-dependent control generation.
sections.details:
Recent VLA models have advanced rapidly, yet jointly training on real-world data, simulation data, and human task videos remains difficult. Different robots have varying numbers of joints and control frequencies; one dataset records relative end-effector displacements, another logs joint angles, and human videos capture skeletal hand keypoints.

Prior approaches typically created separate policies or output heads per robot, used video generation to redraw human hands as robot arms, or applied kinematic retargeting to force actions into robot joint spaces. However, these methods involve massive computational overhead or introduce errors through modeling assumptions, failing to achieve genuine unification.

The authors recognized that the core of manipulation is the geometric relationship directly observable from the camera: where the hand moves relative to objects and how it grasps and transports them. The 3D displacement of two anchor points—the wrist ($p_0$) and the grasp center ($p_1$)—can describe single-arm, dual-arm, humanoid, and human hand motions in the exact same format. UCAG-P sets this shared geometric space as the policy's learning target and delegates executable command generation to a downstream translator, enabling seamless joint training on heterogeneous data.

captions.F2: Comparison of heterogeneous robot learning paradigms. (a) Separate policies per embodiment, (b) End-effector alignment retaining robot-specific control targets, and (c) Our approach (UCAG-P), which shares camera-centric anchor motion across embodiments and translates it into robot-specific commands downstream.

sections.heading: Generalist VLAs, Human Videos, and Action Representations: Where This Work Stands
sections.summary: A review of cross-embodiment learning, robot learning from human video, and action representations. This work introduces novelty by predicting camera-centric geometric motion rather than low-level control values, truly integrating human and heterogeneous robot data without pre-retargeting.
sections.details:
Prior work broadly spans three areas:

- Generalist VLAs and Cross-Embodiment Learning:
Efforts like OpenVLA and Octo pair large-scale datasets with multimodal foundation backbones, but typically rely on embodiment-specific output heads or prompt-based embodiment switching. Recent efforts align into camera-frame end-effector spaces (e.g., Qwen-RobotManip), but cannot directly accommodate human grasping actions.

- Robot Learning from Human Demonstrations:
Human videos are abundant but lack joint-level commands. Conventional methods use them for visual representation pre-training, synthesize robot appearance via video models, or apply inverse kinematics to map hand paths to robot trajectories. In contrast, UCAG-P treats the human hand directly as another embodiment within the shared geometric space, using it as direct policy supervision.

- Action Representations for Manipulation:
Prior studies have explored discrete tokens, diffusion-based trajectory generation, waypoints, and voxels, but most remain tied to specific robot execution formats. UCAG-P structurally separates universally shareable geometric progression from embodiment-specific execution control, setting it apart from existing paradigms.

sections.heading: A 6,300+ Hour Megacorpus: Curating Real-World, Simulated, and Human Demonstrations
sections.summary: A pre-training corpus comprising 11 datasets and 6,373 hours was curated across three pillars: real robots, simulation, and egocentric human manipulation videos. A standardization pipeline maps heterogeneous data into a unified format while masking missing labels.
sections.details:
The training corpus encompasses an unprecedented scale of 1.02 million episodes and 6,373.586 hours. The breakdown is as follows:

- 3.1 Corpus Composition:
Real robot data (DROID, RoboChallenge, RoboCoin, etc.) constitutes 266.3 hours (4.18%), simulation data (RoboCasa GR-1, LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, InternData, etc.) accounts for 3,767.5 hours (59.11%), and egocentric human manipulation videos (VITRA, EgoDex, EgoVerse) contribute 2,339.7 hours (36.71%). Notably, human hand data makes up more than one-third of the total corpus.

- 3.2 Pre-processing and Standardization Pipeline:
Data is transformed into a common format across four stages: episode curation and corruption filtering, image resizing to a unified $224\times 224$ resolution with light color jitter, geometric alignment, and temporal windowing into 30-step chunks ($H=30$). For robot data, forward kinematics and calibration parameters yield camera-frame coordinates for the wrist and gripper center ($p_0, p_1$). For human videos, hand keypoint detectors (e.g., MediaPipe) define the wrist as $p_0$ and the midpoint between thumb and index fingertips as $p_1$.

- 3.3 Role of Graded Supervision:
Different sources provide different annotations; human videos lack joint states, and static cameras lack ego-motion. The pipeline applies loss masks to only the valid dimensions available for each sample, learning directly without synthetically filling missing labels.

captions.F4: Data curation and three-stage training pipeline. Vision-language data and human demonstrations ground shared geometric motion prediction, while simulation and real-robot data progressively optimize the geometry-conditioned translator and executable control generation.

sections.heading: Inside UCAG-P: Two-Stage Anchor Motion Prediction and Geometry-Conditioned Translation
sections.summary: The framework consists of a base policy predicting camera-frame wrist and grasp displacements and a translator converting them into joint commands using robot kinematics. Training occurs across three stages: geometric prediction, standalone translation, and end-to-end integration.
sections.details:
The architecture and training recipe of UCAG-P are cleanly structured:

- 4.1 & 4.2 Camera-Centric Action Space:
The action representation defines two anchors: wrist/effector position $p_0$ and grasp center $p_1$. Over a future horizon of $H=30$ steps at time $t$, the policy predicts camera-frame displacements $\Delta p_0^{\mathrm{cam}}$, $\Delta p_1^{\mathrm{cam}}$, in-plane rotation $\Delta\psi^{\mathrm{cam}}$, and gripper state change $\Delta\gamma^{\mathrm{gripper}}$. A fixed 30-dimensional slot format assigns 10 dimensions to each arm (left and right) and 10 dimensions to camera base displacement, masking unused slots for single-arm systems.

- 4.3 Network Architecture:
The backbone is a VLM (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct). Given images, text instructions, and learnable action queries, an MLP-based motion head decodes the 30-dimensional geometric action chunk from hidden states. Subsequently, the geometry-conditioned action translator ingests the predicted geometric action, current joint states $s_t$, the base-to-camera transformation matrix $T_{\mathrm{base}\leftarrow\mathrm{cam}}$, the local Jacobian $J_t$, and an embodiment token $z_{\mathrm{geo}}$. A Transformer encoder fuses these inputs to produce an 80-dimensional sparse joint command sequence.

- 4.4 Three-Stage Training Pipeline:
In Stage 1, the VLM and motion head are trained on all data (including human videos) to establish robust geometric action prediction. In Stage 2, the action translator is trained standalone using ground-truth geometric trajectories, robot states, and Jacobians. In Stage 3, predicted geometric chunks from the motion head feed into the translator alongside pooled VLM hidden features for joint end-to-end optimization.

- 4.5 Loss Formulation and Inference:
A masked L1 loss computes errors only across valid target dimensions for both geometric motion and executable commands. At test time, camera-frame geometric actions are predicted from vision and language, and the translator maps them into target robot joint commands for downstream controllers.

captions.F6: UCAG-P system architecture and three-stage training details. Left (Stage 1): VLM predicts 30-dimensional camera-centric geometric motion. Top right (Stage 2): Jacobians and coordinate transforms guide translation into 80-dimensional sparse joint commands. Bottom right (Stage 3): End-to-end joint optimization.

sections.heading: One Checkpoint to Move Them All: From Simulation to Real Robots and Human Video Transfer
sections.summary: Evaluated using a single checkpoint without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, UCAG-P reached 98.3% on LIBERO, around 89% on RoboTwin, and 62.0% on RoboCasa. On a real Piper robot, it substantially outperformed baselines in zero-shot transfer from human video.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated how well a single set of model weights generalizes across distinct embodiments and environments:

- Cross-Embodiment Benchmark Performance:
On the single-arm LIBERO benchmark, UCAG-P achieved a 98.3% success rate, matching dedicated specialist models. On dual-arm RoboTwin 2.0, it reached 88.7% on Easy and 89.2% on Hard, significantly outperforming other generalist VLAs. On RoboCasa GR-1, which requires whole-body humanoid control, it reached 62.0%, surpassing the generalist baseline Qwen-VLA (56.7%).

- Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Robustness:
On LIBERO-Plus, which perturbs robot states, lighting, backgrounds, and camera viewpoints, the model maintained an 82.0% zero-shot success rate. Capturing geometric spatial relations provides strong resilience against visual shifts.

- Unseen Embodiment Transfer and Real-World Experiments:
In a zero-shot simulation transfer from ALOHA to the kinematically distinct ARX robot, the model achieved a 35.0% success rate. On a real-world Piper robot, it attained a 60% success rate on a bread-pickup task learning geometric cues purely from human videos (compared to 20% for $\pi_{0.5}$). It also demonstrated superior adaptability on drawer opening (90% vs. 85%) and bowl stacking (75% vs. 65%) over prominent existing VLAs.

captions.F1: Success rate comparisons across major simulation benchmarks: (a) LIBERO, (b) RoboTwin Easy, (c) RoboTwin Hard, and (d) RoboCasa GR-1. Across all benchmarks, UCAG-P uses a single checkpoint without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, approaching or exceeding specialized models.
captions.F7: Task success rates on the real-world Piper robot. Notably in Bread Pickup, which evaluates transfer from human videos, UCAG-P reaches a 60% success rate, substantially outperforming $\pi_0$ and $\pi_{0.5}$.

sections.heading: Takeaways and Next Steps: Scalable Robot Learning via Geometric Alignment
sections.summary: Decoupling camera-centric anchor motion from geometry-conditioned translation proves to be a viable framework for unifying heterogeneous embodiment data. However, reliance on accurate calibration and challenges in transferring across drastically different kinematics remain.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that setting camera-observable geometric motion as a shared target enables unifying single-arm, dual-arm, humanoid, and human demonstration data into a single policy. Incorporating human video without retargeting represents a major step toward overcoming the robot data collection bottleneck.

Nonetheless, clear limitations remain. First, the method relies on precise end-effector poses, camera calibration, and hand keypoint estimation (e.g., MediaPipe); noise or errors in these inputs directly degrade performance. Second, as seen in the 35% success rate during ALOHA-to-ARX transfer, geometric alignment alone struggles to fully bridge significant disparities in joint reach and link lengths (kinematic mismatch). Third, real-robot evaluations remain modest in scale, leaving contact-rich manipulation and extended horizon tasks as important targets for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details, 80-D Command Space, and Failure Analysis
sections.summary: Supplementary details cover network architectures, the 80-dimensional sparse command slot allocation, ablation studies on VLM feature pooling, and an analysis of primary failure modes.
sections.details:
Several technical details provide deeper insight into the framework:

- Sparse Command Slot Design:
The 80-dimensional command vector produced by the translator is partitioned into 10-dimensional blocks. Slots are dedicated to left/right arm joint angles, end-effector poses (XYZ + 6D rotation), left/right gripper commands, waist, and mobile base commands. Unused degrees of freedom for a target embodiment are masked out from both loss computation and control execution.

- Motion Head and Translator Structure:
The motion head projects VLM hidden states (dimension 2,560) to 5,120 dimensions and decodes 30-dimensional geometric actions through a 2-layer residual MLP. The translator applies attention pooling over the full sequence of the final VLM layer using 8 learnable query tokens to inject global visual-linguistic context. Ablations show that adding these pooled VLM features improves RoboCasa GR-1 performance from 58.3% to 62.0% (+3.7 points).

- Failure Mode Analysis:
Failures fall into three primary categories: anchor detection errors, long-horizon trajectory drift, and kinematically infeasible joint configurations produced by the translator. In contact-heavy and kinematically constrained tasks like opening microwave doors (11–13% success on OpenMicrowave), pure geometric motion prediction struggles to account for required torques and interaction constraints.

takeaways: The key to bridging embodiment gaps is predicting camera-frame 3D trajectories of the wrist and grasp center rather than low-level control values.
Human demonstration videos can serve as direct VLA training data as a distinct embodiment by anchoring the wrist and fingertips, eliminating image translation or retargeting.
Decoupling geometric motion prediction (shared VLM) from command generation (geometry-conditioned translator) enables a single policy to control diverse morphologies.
A single model checkpoint without per-benchmark fine-tuning achieves generalization performance competitive with dedicated specialist models.
limitations: Errors in camera calibration, depth estimation, or hand keypoint tracking (e.g., MediaPipe) translate directly into motion errors.
Even with shared geometry, transfer to unseen robots with substantially different link lengths and joint limits (e.g., ALOHA to ARX at 35%) remains challenging.
Pure geometric prediction struggles to maintain proper joint torques and paths in contact-rich, constrained tasks such as opening doors.
